title: Proposal of quantum arrival-time measurement with a Bose-Einstein condensate
authors: Pascal Naidon, Lucas Happ, Denis Boiron
abstract: This work shows how a Bose-Einstein condensate of ultracold atoms could be used to address a long-standing question in quantum theory: how much time does it take for a particle to reach a detector? To this end, we propose a realistic experimental setup, whose key idea is not to measure arrival times directly, but the arrival flux on the detector as a function of its position. This novel approach not only solves practical issues with having a detector close to the system, but also results in signals that allow to unambiguously distinguish different theoretical predictions. This proposal raises prospects for resolving the decades-old debate on this fundamental issue.
summary: The authors propose using Bose-Einstein condensates to experimentally investigate the controversial question of particle arrival time. By measuring the arrival flux at a detector placed far from the source, they circumvent technical limitations and can distinguish between competing theoretical models for quantum transport. This provides a powerful testbed connecting fundamental theory with advanced cold atom experiments.
main_problem: The work addresses the fundamental, long-standing quantum mechanical question of determining the time taken for a particle to travel between two points.
main_result: A novel experimental setup using Bose-Einstein condensates can measure the arrival flux at a distant detector, allowing unambiguous discrimination between various theoretical predictions for arrival-time distributions.
method: The methodology proposes measuring the arrival flux on a detector placed far from the source, rather than attempting direct time measurement near the source to avoid back-action and technical limitations.
model_or_system: The physical system is a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) of ultracold atoms. The dynamics are governed by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, and the experiment utilizes the BEC's expansion as it falls towards a detector.
key_observables: The primary observable is the average number of detected counts on the detector as a function of its horizontal position ($\Delta x$), which reveals the arrival flux distribution $\Pi(t)$.
important_parameters: Key parameters include the total atom number ($N$) and trapping frequencies ($\omega_{\parallel}, \omega_{\perp}$), with noise reduction requiring averaging over many experimental runs.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that measurements can be performed far from the source to minimize disturbance, and that sufficient averaging is possible to overcome shot noise obscuring predicted oscillations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the limitations of standard near-source detection versus the proposed distant setup. Supplementary figures demonstrate how increasing atom number ($N$) and averaging over many experiments are necessary to reveal small oscillatory patterns predicted by axiomatic approaches.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical ambiguity regarding arrival time measurements, then details the practical limitations of existing setups (Fig 1a). It proposes a novel, distant detection scheme using BECs (Fig 1b), discusses observable diagnostics ($\Delta x$ dependence), and finally analyzes the feasibility of detecting subtle quantum effects like oscillations via noise analysis.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it merges fundamental theoretical questions about quantum dynamics with cutting-edge experimental techniques in cold atom physics, providing a concrete roadmap for testing foundational quantum concepts.

figures.caption: Figure 1. (a) Standard arrival-time experiment. (b) Our experimental setup proposal. In both cases, a vertical and a horizontal laser beams form an optical dipole trap in which a cloud of metastable helium-4 atoms is trapped – here, it is illustrated for configuration (1) of the lasers, which produces a vertical cigar-shaped cloud. At some time, the cloud is released by switching off laser 2 (a) or both laser beams (b). In our proposal (b), the cloud falls into a lower chamber where it can be detected on a horizontal and a vertical microchannel plate detector.
